channel.title: Noticias del Mundo — Ciencia
channel.description: Noticias de ciencia de todas las fuentes configuradas.

item.title: Spectral clues suggest hollow-core magnetic jet in brightest-ever gamma-ray burst
item.description: A China–Italy joint research team has reconstructed the time-resolved spectrum of GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma-ray burst (GRB) ever observed, and proposed that the burst may have produced a magnetically dominated jet with a hollow core. This is presented as a possible interpretation of the emission line's rise-then-fall evolution rather than a direct detection. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country
item.description: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
item.description: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing during first year at sea
item.description: New research has revealed young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing in their epic first year at sea, strengthening the case for proposed new marine protected areas. The study was co-led by France's CNRS, the Center Scientifique de Monaco and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The international research team tracked 48 juvenile emperor penguins from three colonies around the Weddell Sea: Snow Hill Island, Jason Peninsula and Atka Bay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Portland architect's flower-shaped forest home lists for $2.888 million
item.description: A unique forest home in Portland designed by architect Robert Oshatz is now listed at $2.888 million. The property features curved ceilings and disappearing glass walls that blend living space with nature. It includes four bedrooms, four bathrooms, and multiple levels accessible by an elevator. The home is part of a larger planned collection of residences sharing forested land. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Yes, men and boys should be shamed for misogyny. It's part of how we stamp it out
item.description: The headlines of recent weeks and months have been dominated by men accused of doing terrible things to women. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild barley's genetic diversity opens up new avenues for research and breeding
item.description: For the first time, an international research team coordinated by the IPK Leibniz Institute has characterized genomic diversity across the agriculturally important genus Hordeum. The study reveals how the genomes of barley and its wild relatives have evolved. These findings open up new avenues for systematically investigating this diversity and, in the long term, utilizing it for plant breeding. The results are published in the journal Nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Insects on these sub‑Antarctic islands are bouncing back after invasive rats and mice were eradicated
item.description: Island species typically evolve in isolation—and often without many predators. As a result, islands are home to high numbers of unique species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Learning science one virtual escape room at a time
item.description: Albert Einstein's ghost is trapped inside a science laboratory, and he needs help escaping. Fortunately, a group of seventh graders is up to the challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In Antarctica's ice‑free areas, even footprints can damage rare microscopic ecosystems
item.description: The usual advice for people visiting wilderness areas is to leave nothing but footprints. But as our new study shows, even footprints may disturb rare ecosystems in Antarctica and cause irreversible changes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Psychology says a few minutes of your speech may reveal how fast your brain is aging
item.description: A groundbreaking speech clock has been developed by researchers to evaluate speech patterns and estimate biological age. This innovative tool highlights the potential relationship between speech traits and cognitive decline, including dementia. Involving nearly 3,000 Spanish-speaking participants from various Latin American nations, the results suggest that noticeable differences in speech age may signal cognitive difficulties. Future research is essential to further explore the role of speech analysis in cognitive evaluations. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Electrified fabric captures phosphate for potential recovery from wastewater
item.description: When rain falls on farmland, lawns and gardens, it can wash phosphate from fertilizers into nearby waterways, triggering harmful algal blooms that cloud lakes and rivers, release toxins and rob the water of oxygen needed to sustain aquatic life. Now, Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory researchers have developed a reusable electrode that captures phosphate from water in laboratory tests, potentially recovering a valuable, nonrenewable resource while reducing water pollution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As Americans gather for Thanksgiving, a centuries‑old Sikh tradition offers an expansive vision of hospitality
item.description: On Sundays at Gurdwara Guru Nanaksar in Chapin, South Carolina, diners sit in rows on the floor while volunteers walk along each row carrying pots and trays of food. They pause to offer each person a spoonful of dal, a dish made with lentils, or a serving of vegetables. When the roti—a kind of flatbread—comes around, diners hold out both hands, palms up. A volunteer places the bread directly into their hands. This is "langar," the free communal meal served at Sikh houses of worship around the world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Data centres could ignite a 'climate bomb' in Australia, report finds
item.description: The Climate Council has identified nine proposed data centres in Australia that could produce up to 40 million tonnes of pollution a year by 2035 if powered by fossil fuels. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Grace Nakamura and Danielle Pope

item.title: Using light to switch molecular states in the smallest of spaces
item.description: What if light could be used not just to observe matter, but to actively reprogram it? Photochromic materials contain molecules that switch between distinct molecular states when exposed to different colors of light. This ability offers exciting possibilities for optical memory and light-controlled electronic devices. However, controlling these molecular changes within extremely small spaces remains challenging because conventional optics cannot focus light to dimensions much smaller than its wavelength. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new life cycle assessment of polyethylene packaging and alternatives in the US and Europe
item.description: A new research study assessed five major PE packaging applications and organized the analysis around three germane, current questions. How does PE compare with paper, glass, and metal alternatives? How do reuse, post-consumer recycled content, and end-of-life recycling affect the potential environmental impact results? What happens when package-level differences scale to projected demand through 2030 and beyond? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Migrating moth uses Earth's magnetic field as a compass
item.description: Every year, the bogong moth sets off on long migrations through the night. To find its way, it uses the stars as a guide. Now, a new study from Lund University shows that, like migratory birds, the moth also has a built-in magnetic compass that helps it stay on course. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth after 49 years in space
item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached a record distance of more than 16 billion miles from Earth, 49 years after its launch. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: Crystal layers just 10 nanometers thick assemble into a tiny tunable grid
item.description: Researchers have fabricated two ultrathin crystal sheets that, when stacked and rotated relative to each other, create a square lattice of defects at their interface. These defects change how electrical charges are arranged, and when the 10-nanometer-thick sheets are bonded and twisted, tiny electrical patterns emerge at the interface. These controllable arrangements could eventually prove useful in the electronics industry, although using them in a working device will require further research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Inflated receipts and fake loans: Giving to charities to evade tax
item.description: Some taxpayers use charitable donations to illegally reduce their taxes, using schemes orchestrated by promoters and supported by financial advisers and charities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists send an unblockable message using gravity
item.description: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Damaged rocks may help explain why small earthquakes outnumber large ones
item.description: University of Michigan researchers have developed a better way to understand why earthquakes occur and what size they might be. Currently, models that predict earthquakes only account for slipping that occurs along a main fault, activity that usually generates large earthquakes. Instead, the U-M researchers have built a model that considers not only the main fault action but also the activity of rocks that lie adjacent to the fault and become damaged during earthquake events. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MAF EAP – Holidays – How to manage the BAH HUMBUG that tries to sneak in
item.description: Holidays are often a fun break during a busy year – a long weekend here and there is an event many of us can get behind. However, when a short holiday break turns into a full holiday season, we know that this is a different “ball game”. Everyone has stress about something – some people […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Justin M. Robert

item.title: Water purification method turns old batteries into magnetic pollutant traps
item.description: How can harmful substances be removed from water? When it comes to dyes that cannot simply be filtered out, this is usually very laborious: You need substances to which the dyes attach, and then the water often has to be painstakingly centrifuged. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How cells use alternative genetic instructions to produce 'shadowing proteins'
item.description: The human genome contains tens of thousands of genes that provide instructions for making the proteins responsible for carrying out essential functions throughout the body. But those instructions may be more versatile than scientists once understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Strange radio signals from space could come from a dead star
item.description: The night sky is as good a place as any for a mystery. Back in 2002, astronomer Scott Hyman and his colleagues detected five mysterious bursts of radio waves coming from near the center of our galaxy, spaced roughly 77 minutes apart. The signals were detected again in 2003 and 2004, but then disappeared. Despite years of searching, there was no sign of their return. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers review isotope methods for tracing and quantifying gaseous nitrogen production in soils
item.description: Researchers from the Institute of Applied Ecology (IAE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have reviewed stable nitrogen isotope techniques for tracing the sources and quantifying the production of gaseous nitrogen in soils. The review examines four approaches for distinguishing microbial pathways that produce nitrous oxide (N₂O), nitric oxide (NO) and dinitrogen (N₂). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stem cell–derived nanoparticles modulate immune cells and help delay type 1 diabetes in mice
item.description: In people with type 1 diabetes, the immune system mistakenly identifies insulin-producing cells in the pancreas as foreign and attacks them, leaving the body unable to properly regulate blood sugar. While insulin therapy helps manage the disease, it does not stop the underlying immune attack. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Announces Mid-Power Electric Rocket Challenge for US Companies
item.description: NASA launched a new competition inviting U.S. companies to produce prototypes of mid-power Hall effect thrusters – a type of electric propulsion system considered crucial for future space operations and exploration. Hall effect thrusters use an electric field to accelerate a propellant gas, producing efficient thrust for long-duration missions. Used for propelling satellites and deep […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Bailey Light

item.title: Bolivia's Madidi National Park shelters 99 bat species, including 7 new to the country
item.description: A new study has confirmed 100 bat taxa in Madidi National Park, in northwestern Bolivia, including 99 recognized species and one that may be new to science. The park is home to 68% of the bat species known from Bolivia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Making diversity count: New paper highlights overlooked scientists in the chemical sciences curriculum
item.description: A new paper by James Wilton-Ely, Ravi Singh and collaborators explores how curriculum diversification can help address the underrepresentation of minority-background scientists in chemical sciences education. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Empire State Building Goes Gold for Voyager
item.description: The Empire State Building is seen illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft as it was about to pass one light-day away from Earth, a distance reached by no other human-made object, Nov. 17, 2026. The color gold represents the gold-plated copper phonograph record that is flying on Voyager; the Golden Record contains […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Record ocean warming hundreds of meters below B.C. coast linked to El Niño
item.description: Scientists are observing record ocean temperatures off the British Columbia coast, with temperatures spiking as much as 2.5 degrees Celsius above the long-term averages recorded at Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) seafloor observatory sites—indicating the arrival of El Niño impacts on Canada's Pacific coastline. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bee-lieve it or not, bumblebees have a sweet spot for salt
item.description: Minerals are vital for bumblebee health, but too much can be harmful. For this new study, which is published in Royal Society Open Science, researchers tested how buff-tailed bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) responded to different levels of calcium, potassium, magnesium and sodium in artificial nectar. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What Is the Moon Base?
item.description: This article is for students. NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost. It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore. ______________________________________________________________________ Words to Know outpost: a station or base located in […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlyn Adams

item.title: Thank You for Doing NASA Science!
item.description: It’s Thanksgiving time, and we’re giving thanks to you for doing NASA Science with us! You and NASA’s other volunteers have enabled an incredible banquet of discoveries—by taking data, analyzing data, writing code, writing papers, and even inventing your own science projects. Whether you’re an expert participant or someone who’s just started your science journey, […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Writing changes language less than we think
item.description: Writing is one of the most important inventions in human history. It transformed how we share knowledge, communicate and pass information from one generation to the next. But has it also changed the way we build sentences and the complexity of our languages? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Miniaturization found at the origin of amphibians opens new ecological territory
item.description: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians—the three groups of living amphibians—together number more than 9,000 species. On average, they are the smallest of all four-limbed vertebrates, and some are extremely small: Brachycephalus toads measure less than 7 millimeters (0.28 inches) from snout to vent. Their ancient relatives were very different animals. Most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians (lissamphibians) arose, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters (3.3 to 16.4 feet) long. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Muslims to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, study finds
item.description: Demographic patterns suggest Christianity’s center will move to Africa, and America will no longer be majority-Christian, new research finds. Fuente: The Washington Post - World.
item.dc:creator: Michelle Boorstein

item.title: NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger
item.description: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: La NASA va a estrenar el telescopio Roman por todo lo alto y te ofrece que adoptes uno de los píxeles de sus primeras imágenes
item.description: El pasado 30 de agosto, la NASA lanzó con éxito el Nancy Grace Roman, el telescopio que pretende convertirse en el detective de la materia oscura . Desde entonces, todo ha sido una sucesión de buenas noticias. Cada maniobra fue mucho más precisa que en el mejor de los escenarios previstos, por lo que ahorró combustible para 12 años adicionales. Las primeras imágenes de prueba que se enviaron a medida que calibraba sus instrumentos tuvieron un rendimiento muy bueno, a pesar de no haber alineado aún todos sus espejos. En general, el Roman, como se le conoce coloquialmente, ha superado todas las… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: La COP31 encara su recta final con negociaciones intensas y desacuerdos profundos
item.description: Combustibles fósiles, dinero y ciencia son algunos de los temas sobre los que las delegaciones reunidas en la COP31 de Turquía seguían debatiendo este miércoles para tratar de salvar una declaración política que mantenga altas las ambiciones climáticas. El borrador inicial del lunes había chocado con el rechazo de la Unión Europea, que lo calificó de "lista de la compra". Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: France 24

item.title: Otro hito espacial de la Voyager 1: la NASA confirma que es el primer objeto lanzado por el hombre a un día luz de la Tierra
item.description: La sonda fue lanzada en 1977 y recorre el espacio interestelar tras salir del sistema solar Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Business Council of Australia more aligned with fossil fuel industry than its members’ values, analysis finds
item.description: Research by InfluenceMap raises questions about association’s policies and representation, particularly around advocacy for new gas supplies Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies. The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Barrett Business editor

item.title: Why does the same perfume smell different on different people? 'Skin chemistry' explained
item.description: Have you ever sprayed a perfume on a paper strip in a department store and loved the smell, only to find it didn't perform the same when you sprayed it on your skin? It's a common experience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a toxin helps African lungfish survive on land
item.description: For centuries, scientists have been fascinated by critical steps in animal evolution, such as the advent of multicellularity or the ability to fly. One such evolutionary step many have heard about is vertebrate adaptation to land. Adventuring onto land is one of the best-known stories of vertebrate success, a strategy that drove their diversification. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Link between social media use and veterans' democracy concerns identified
item.description: Post-9/11 veterans who used minimally moderated, ideologically oriented social media platforms reported greater concern about the condition of U.S. democracy and less satisfaction with the end of the war in Afghanistan than veterans who used other social media platforms or no social media at all, according to a new study by Penn State researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What happens when AI takes the human out of human resources?
item.description: When a company decides whom to hire, promote or lay off, how much of that decision should be left to artificial intelligence? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a rare, potentially life-threatening inflammatory disorder is driven by malfunctioning immune cells, overturning three decades of scientific understanding. The breakthrough points to a promising new treatment using existing medications, with one severely affected infant already showing substantial improvement. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12
item.description: Scientists have found a surprising new use for vitamin B12, developing a rechargeable battery that uses the essential nutrient to help generate and store electricity. The prototype survived up to 250 charging cycles and could open the door to safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly alternatives to lithium-ion batteries. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Greener living? It's all in the scheduling
item.description: A research team led by Professor Inseok Hwang of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at POSTECH, including integrated MS-Ph.D. students Jeongwon Choi and Donghyeon Kang, has developed EcoTailor, a mobile planning system that suggests actionable low-carbon daily schedules tailored to users' commitments, transportation options and personal preferences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
item.description: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
item.description: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now one light-day away
item.description: After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: the spacecraft is now officially one light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, "very, very far." The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET, and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our […] Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: Jess Weatherbed

item.title: “Subíos a mi carro cislunar”: la Fuerza Espacial estadounidense busca aliados para vigilar el espacio entre la Tierra y la Luna
item.description: En diciembre de 2025, Donald Trump emitió una orden ejecutiva que contempla detectar, caracterizar y contrarrestar amenazas en el espacio cislunar. Lógicamente, esto llamó la atención de algunos expertos en derecho espacial, pues podría atentar contra el Tratado del Espacio Exterior , en el que se prohíbe que cualquier Estado se apropie de la Luna u otros cuerpos celestes, ya sea por reclamación de soberanía, uso u ocupación. Es cierto que vigilar y protegerse contra amenazas no iría contra esta norma, pero sí que pone sobre la mesa el tema de un posible conflicto por la posesión de nuestro… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Using a microwave link to transfer a three-level quantum state
item.description: Quantum technologies, devices and systems that process, store, transfer or collect information leveraging the laws of quantum mechanics, could outperform their classical counterparts on some real-world tasks. Many of these technologies encode quantum information in qubits, which can exist in either of two basic states or a superposition of them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Field of fire: Chinese scientists develop drone gun that can plant rice more efficiently
item.description: For years, engineers around the world have experimented with mounting guns on drones to boost battlefield firepower. But a new study by Chinese researchers shows that unmanned vehicles could be used to shoot a very different kind of ammunition – rice. In a paper published last month, the researchers detailed an optimised pump system that could use precise, high-pressure jets to plant rice rather than randomly scattering the seeds. “This study proposes a seed-metering pump designed for a... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Bela

item.title: Can natural soybean varieties handle dicamba drift? New study tests promising lines
item.description: Some soybean growers who plant genetically modified dicamba-resistant soybeans have no intention of spraying the herbicide. Among other reasons, they're hedging against damaging dicamba exposure arising from neighboring fields. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA Voyager 1 probe believed to have reached ‘light-day’ milestone
item.description: The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, ‌the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 26 billion km Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: Genomic breakthrough offers new hope for southern corroboree frog
item.description: Researchers have shown for the first time that genomic selection—a breeding technique widely used in agriculture—could help one of Australia's most threatened frogs become more resilient to a deadly disease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Art experiments reveal artists' intuitive grasp of what makes images memorable
item.description: Why do some artworks stick in our minds, while others fade away soon after we view them? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’? |
item.description: Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering. Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.
item.dc:creator: Kim Heacox

item.title: El test genético que descubrió el covid-19 y que ahora salva vidas al detectar casi todas las infecciones
item.description: Permitió identificar el covid-19. Ahora, esta técnica genética ayuda a los médicos a tomar decisiones de vida o muerte. Fuente: BBC News Mundo.

item.title: SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site unless ministers intervene
item.description: Large North Sea operator EnQuest says it is quitting oil basin, while SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site Nils Pratley: with more gas storage at risk. What’s the government plan for secure supplies? The energy secretary has been dealt a double blow after two UK companies signalled plans to pull their investment from large fossil fuel projects amid disagreements over government policies. One of the North Sea’s biggest independent companies, EnQuest, said on Wednesday it was quitting the North Sea oil and gas basin to focus on making better returns in Asia, blaming the “uncertain… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Joanna Partridge

item.title: Scientists warn of growing health threats of chemicals found everywhere
item.description: Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sudden heat spikes harm honey bees more than sustained heat, study finds
item.description: A sudden heat shock can be harmful to honey bees, but as a heat wave goes on, bees adapt and the high temperatures are less destructive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eagles preying on human-sized baboons upend existing evolutionary defense theory
item.description: Researchers from the University of St Andrews have discovered that baboons the size of hominins (early human ancestors) are being preyed upon by eagles, reshaping the way scientists might think about predator–prey interactions during human evolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
item.description: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 18 – An M-class Solar Flare
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 18 – An… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Medium-Sized […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Sierra Snow Season Spins Up
item.description: A widespread, early-season snowstorm blanketed California’s mountains in white in mid-November 2026. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
item.description: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Houston leads large metros in child poverty, disconnected youth
item.description: Houston is one of the nation's largest economic engines, but for many of its youngest residents, the path to financial stability begins with significant obstacles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment
item.description: Scientists have developed a new technique that uses magnetic nanoparticles to stimulate deep brain regions, dramatically improving Parkinson’s-like movement problems in mice without permanently implanted electrodes. The breakthrough could pave the way for less invasive treatments using injectable particles and wearable magnetic headbands. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Photon fluctuations offer new way to probe electron dynamics in crystals
item.description: Intense laser light can make a crystal emit new colors at frequencies many times higher than that of the original beam. This process, known as high-harmonic generation, provides a powerful way to investigate the rapid motion of electrons in solids. Researchers usually study the brightness and spectrum of the emitted light. Yet those measurements capture only part of the available information. Fluctuations between individual laser pulses can also reveal how the emission is produced. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New model reveals how water moves through tile-drained farm fields
item.description: Tile drainage fundamentally alters how water moves through agricultural fields, affecting surface ponding, water-table dynamics, crop growth, nutrient transport and water quality. Yet fields with similar drainage systems can respond differently depending on soil, topography and tile design—differences that most models struggle to resolve at the field scale. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
item.description: NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New research finds AI adoption is associated with more managers—and different managerial skills
item.description: A Strategic Management Journal study challenges the assumption that AI adoption automatically reduces demand for managers. Liudmila Alekseeva, José Azar, Mireia Giné and Sampsa Samila analyze U.S. job postings from 2010 to 2022, linking firm-level AI adoption with managerial vacancies and skill requirements. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
item.description: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Gender differences in values are not widening in Europe after all
item.description: In recent years, public discussion has focused on the increasingly conservative values of young men. A recently published study indicates that this is primarily a phenomenon prominent in social and conventional media, not an overall trend. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How restaurants can make sustainable dining choices easier while still making a profit
item.description: Canadians are eating out less. A 2025 survey found 57% of them are cooking at home more often to save money, while 69% of restaurant operators say customers are dining out less because of affordability. According to Restaurants Canada, 41% of operators are either losing money or breaking even. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
item.description: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese scientists’ magic comb restores hair growth by nearly 100% in mice study
item.description: For the more than 1.5 billion people worldwide who suffer from androgenetic alopecia, combing their hair before the mirror each morning is a routine that is often accompanied by quiet anxiety. However, this most ordinary everyday tool may hold the key to reversing hair loss, according to a Chinese research team which developed a comb that uses microelectronics to treat hair loss. A study on mice has found that nearly 100 per cent hair coverage was achieved in just 28 days using the device,... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Shi Huang

item.title: Writing as it should be or as it sounds: Reconstructing how Old English disappeared
item.description: In the twelfth century, the English-speaking world underwent a major change: Old English gave way to Middle English. In his dissertation, Ph.D. candidate Amos van Baalen uses sermons to reconstruct how this change took place. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How do human lifestyles affect the gut microbiome of our canine companions?
item.description: Dogs have been living side by side with humans for millennia, but a new study underscores how much we have yet to learn about man's best friend. The study, which looked at hundreds of dogs across four nations, found that the lifestyles of pet owners appear to play a significant role in determining what constitutes a healthy gut microbiome for their dog companions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How machine learning can tackle lead pipe challenges
item.description: A new machine learning tool developed through the Centre for Resilience in Environment, Water and Waste (CREWW) could help water companies identify properties most likely to be connected to lead service pipes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hugh Jackman, Rebel Wilson and 150 Australian artists join call to block Woodside gas development near Scott Reef
item.description: Actors, authors and musicians sign open letter urging Murray Watt to reject the fossil fuel company’s plan to drill for gas in Browse basin off Kimberley coast Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here More than 150 Australian artists, including Hugh Jackman, Rebel Wilson and Jessica Mauboy, have backed a Greenpeace-led campaign against Woodside Energy’s proposal to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast. Woodside, the country’s largest fossil fuel company, describes Browse as “Australia’s biggest undeveloped offshore gas… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Donna Lu

item.title: Study tracks what students learn from online teamwork and fieldwork abroad
item.description: Can a solution that cuts food waste in Tokyo work in Seoul too? Exploring a familiar problem with peers abroad can help students question what they take for granted at home and see how their knowledge might apply to real-world sustainability challenges. As educators put time and care into designing international courses, what do students take away from the experience, and what stays with them after the course ends? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum-gas microscope resolves the 'color' of individual atoms in a single shot
item.description: In 2024, researchers at the Ultracold Quantum Gases group at ICFO built a quantum-gas microscope capable of imaging individual atoms in strontium quantum gases for the first time, marking a key enabling step for quantum simulation. At that time, the researchers imaged strontium-84, a boson that has no spin. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How to make AI data centres more sustainable
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03708-6 Tech companies and governments face opposition over data centres’ expansion, in part because of their huge power requirements. They must not be powered with fossil fuels. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: At-home microbiome tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03710-y Our reporter mailed off her poo to find out what two companies say about her microbiome. Here’s what she found. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Are you a budding science sleuth? Take our plagiarism quiz to test your skills
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03040-z Sleuths and publishers seize on ‘tortured phrases’ to detect research fraud. Sometimes they can raise a smile. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Conference networking made simple, in three short videos
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03678-9 Working the room is a skill you can practise and prepare for. Here’s how. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: First observation of a giant star swallowing its neighbour
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03784-8 Finding provides new insights into what happens within stellar mergers — plus, using quantum physics to securely pinpoint someone’s location. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Nick Petrić Howe

item.title: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03602-1 Global agricultural demand has increased over the past few decades, driving land-use intensification in some of the world’s most biodiverse regions. An assessment of some 40,000 species, from soil microorganisms to vertebrates, in Sumatra, Indonesia, reveals that agricultural intensification threatens biodiversity through species loss and changes in community composition across different spatial scales. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Kings of the jungle? This early human had surprising survival skills that rivalled ours
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03777-7 Teeth found in south China challenge the idea that Homo erectus was limited to woodlands and savannahs. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Intra-stellar: a star inside a giant star
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03273-y Long-term monitoring of a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy reveals, for the first time, the decay of the orbit of another star inside the giant’s envelope. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Jason Nordhaus

item.title: Glucose-powered implant brings devices for treating diabetes a step closer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03377-5 A device that stimulates the main nerve between the brain and the internal organs when blood sugar is high is an effective therapy in rat models of diabetes. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11427-1 Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Liu

item.title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03436-x Large and giant DNA viruses that infect unicellular eukaryotes are abundant in the environment but have rarely been found in the gut microbiome. The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Meet ‘egoviruses’: the surprise microbes living in the guts of millions of people
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03766-w Egoviruses could be the evolutionary missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and those that can infect people. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Fieldhouse

item.title: A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03490-5 Much of the Amazon rainforest was thought to be evergreen, but high-resolution satellite imagery reveals that many of its trees can remain leafless for longer than expected. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Gerbrand Koren

item.title: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03599-7 When migratory locusts are injured, an odorous chemical produced by bacteria living in or on their bodies activates the immune system, helping them to fight disease-causing agents. However, when a wound is large and the chemical becomes too concentrated, it attracts cannibalistic locusts. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03717-5 Technology companies can’t be the judges of their own regulatory compliance. Centuries of history explain why. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: A grant to hand out more grants — and build a research area
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03689-6 A rapid microgrants scheme called the Field Building Accelerator aims to launch new scientific fields. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Virginia Gewin

item.title: Quantum physics can prove where you are
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03378-4 Demonstrating your location to someone far away is surprisingly hard. Quantum correlations offer a way to do so without needing to trust any quantum hardware. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Davide Bacco

item.title: The right to do wrong
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03517-x An equal chance. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11284-y A basin-wide assessment of Amazonian deciduousness using high-resolution satellite observations shows a diverse range of phenological strategies across the Amazon rainforest, contrary to the prevailing view of Amazonian phenology. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Jin Wu

item.title: Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11289-7 A transition from continuous to periodic pulsed superradiant emission in coupled spin–resonator systems is demonstrated, revealing connections to time crystals and enabling synchronized microwave and optical frequency combs. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Faraon

item.title: Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11100-7 Frameworks for corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains; the scientific community has a role in developing robust, actionable frameworks for corporate decarbonization. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Niklas Höhne

item.title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11268-y Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time) is realized using two coherently coupled spin components in a two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11251-7 NeuroAxis restores glucose tolerance, improves insulin sensitivity and normalizes glycaemic control, with therapeutic effects persisting after treatment cessation in rat models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11270-4 A pan-cancer single-cell analysis of the tumour microenvironment across 42 cancer types and across 2 species is described. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3 A loophole-free Bell-test quantum protocol demonstrates secure, device-independent position verification, achieving up to 4.53-fold smaller localization volumes than classical methods and enabling tamper-resistant location-based authentication. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Lynden K. Shalm

item.title: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11294-w A defect-free unitary Fermi gas is used in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Tilman Esslinger

item.title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11299-5 A fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings the functionalities of fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification together in a single-step-grown platform is shown. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Sanvitto

item.title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11235-7 TransA-MERFISH combines anterograde trans-neuronal tracing and spatial transcriptomics and reveals distinct retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cell-dependent and independent motion-selective pathways in superior colliculus, establishing a sensitive cell-type-resolved framework for wiring-diagram reconstruction in early visual processing. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Xin Duan

item.title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11254-4 An architecture comprising monolayer graphene doubly aligned to bulk and monolayer hBN on either side shows a gate-tunable global structural phase transition between two stacking configurations, accompanied by flat-band-induced integer doping. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: K. S. Novoselov

item.title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11155-6 Eight Homo erectus teeth from two caves in southern China reveal that the species persisted in closed rainforest ecosystems between 324 and 184 ka, challenging assumptions about their ecological preferences and behavioural limitations. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Y. Zhang

item.title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
item.description: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11322-9 During their biannual migration, nocturnal Bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) rely on both a stellar and a geomagnetic compass for navigation, enabling them to maintain their migratory direction even if one of these cues is missing. Fuente: Nature.
